How does the German government work? Is it like the UK, where the PM is chosen by the majority party?

Short Version: Yes, the chancellor de facto is always installed by the current majority party.

Long Version:

Every four years, the federal present (a largely formal role) suggests a chancellor candidate, based on previous talks with all majority parties (usually the Christian Democrats and the Social Democracts). The chancellor candidate then has to gain the majority of all votes from all German federal MPs via secret ballot.

If the chancellor candidate suggested by the president does not gain the necessary majority, the parliament may suggest its own nominee over a fourteen-day span, who also needs to get the majority vote of all federal MPs.

If this second candidate also fails to gain a majority, the individual parties send in their own candidates (rather then trying to collectively agree on one), and the candidate the gains the most votes (relatively, not absolute) is propped up as the new chancellor candidate. If this new candidate gets the absolute majority of all federal MP votes, he or she automatically becomes chancellor. If not, the federal president may either choose to make the candidate with the highest individual votes chancellor, or may dissolve the Bundestag to start new elections.

This being said: No chancellor candidate suggested by the federal president has failed to gain the majority of federal MP votes in the entire history of Germany (starting with the independence of West-Germany in 1949.

In the event that the current chancellor proves to be completely incompetent, the federal parliament may also start a constructive vote of no-confidence, that is: If parliament can agree on a new chancellor candidate and said candidate gets more than half of all German federal MP votes, said candidate immediately replaces the acting chancellor.
